Issue no. 8

Trash orresource?

It depends on what we do with it!

Come with Tampinha, the scrap robot, to get to know, sort, transform and take care. There are 15 games along the way!

The Portuguese version has a Brazilian Sign Language (Libras) translation.

Theme 1

I know

Beep, beep! I'm Tampinha. I was built from a can, bottle caps, a spring and screws that someone was going to throw away. Lots of people call everything they throw out trash. But the right name is solid waste. Do you know why? Because almost everything is still good for something!

Waste from homes and from street cleaning makes up urban solid waste (BRASIL, 2010). For collection, it is sorted into three groups:

  • Dry recyclablesPaper, plastic, glass and metal. They become new products.
  • Organic wasteFood and plant scraps. They become fertilizer.
  • Landfill wasteWhat can't be used anymore.

Trash or waste?

There are 8 cards per round. Look at each piece of waste and say which group it belongs to. Then Tampinha explains why. Get 6 right to earn the star.

What does the law say?

Brazil's National Solid Waste Policy (Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos) calls only what can no longer be used or recycled landfill waste. And it recognizes that recyclable waste is a good that has value and creates jobs and income (BRASIL, 2010).

Sorting into three groups, dry recyclables, organic waste and landfill waste, is the rule for recycling collection throughout the country (BRASIL, 2022).

Did you know?

About half the waste in Brazilian cities is organic: food and plant scraps (BRASIL, 2017).

Before becoming waste, everything was a product. And before being a product, it was a piece of nature: a tree, sand, ore, oil. Shall we find out where each material comes from?

Where does it come from?

Tap an object on the left, then its raw material on the right. A raw material is what nature provides to make the object.

Sources: Indústria Brasileira de Árvores ([2026]), Associação Brasileira da Indústria do Plástico ([2019]), Associação Brasileira das Indústrias de Vidro ([20--]), São Paulo (2024), Beltrão (2006) and Instituto Aço Brasil ([2021]).

Oops! And what about the waste that escapes and ends up on the street, in the river and in the sea? Plastic doesn't disappear. It keeps breaking into smaller and smaller pieces. Grab the magnifying glass and come investigate with me!

Microplastic detectives

Microplastics are bits of plastic so small you can barely see them. Tap each question mark and use Tampinha's magnifying glass to find out where they come from and where they go.

Clues found: 0 of 7

Sources: United Nations Environment Programme (2021, 2025) and Zorzetto (2025).

Theme 2

I sort

Mixed waste is hard to use. Sorted waste becomes raw material, which is the material used to make new things! When already-sorted waste is picked up, that's called recycling collection. In many places, the bins have colors, one for each material. Do you know them all?

The colors of recycling

Look at the waste on the tray and tap the right bin. Each bin has a color, a symbol and a name. Get 7 of 10 right on the first try to earn the star!

Item 1 of 10 Right on the first try: 0
On the tray

Which bin does it go in?

There are four more colors

They're not in this game, but they're good to know.

    The ten colors are in CONAMA Resolution No. 275 (Resolução CONAMA nº 275) (CONSELHO NACIONAL DO MEIO AMBIENTE, 2001). Your city may do it differently: many sort into three groups, which are dry recyclables, organic waste and landfill waste (BRASIL, 2022). The city government decides.

    How do you prepare recyclables?

    Recyclable materials should go to collection clean and dry (BRASIL, 2013). So remove food scraps from packaging and don't get the paper wet.

    Broken glass is dangerous. An adult takes care of it.

    Watch out! Some waste can't go in the home bin: batteries, expired medicine, broken phones, fluorescent bulbs, used cooking oil. Each one has a right place to be dropped off. An adult takes them, but you can help remind them!

    Proper disposal

    Some waste doesn't go in the home bin or in regular recycling collection. It has its own drop-off point. Look at the item and tap the place in the neighborhood where an adult should take it. One place can take more than one kind of waste.

    Right drop-offs: 0 of 8
    Item 1 of 8 Expired medicine

    Drop-off points change from city to city. Ask at the city hall or at the shops in your neighborhood.

    Do you know who makes recycling happen? Waste pickers (in Brazil, catadoras and catadores). They collect, sort and sell materials to factories. Many work together, in cooperatives. Shall we get to know their work?

    At the cooperative

    Today you visit the cooperative and help the waste pickers, just pretend. Look at what comes along the conveyor belt and tap the right destination. Each material has its own bulk bag, which is a very big sack.

    1. 1Sorting
    2. 2Press
    3. 3General store
    12 items left
    The belt is about to start.

    The occupation of waste picker has been recognized in the Brazilian Classification of Occupations since 2002 (SILVA; GOES; ALVAREZ, 2013). The National Solid Waste Policy (Política Nacional de Resíduos Sólidos) encourages cooperatives (BRASIL, 2010), and a federal program supports this work (BRASIL, 2023). Other sources: Associação Brasileira da Indústria do PET ([20--]b) and Instituto Aço Brasil ([2021]).

    What does the law say?

    Brazilian law says that city recycling collection must give priority to waste picker cooperatives (BRASIL, 2010). Since 2023, a federal government program has supported this work (BRASIL, 2023).

    I transform

    Now comes my favorite part: transforming! In recycling, used material becomes raw material and then a new product. Paper becomes paper, glass becomes glass, a can becomes a can. Choose a material and follow its journey.

          Before recycling, it's worth asking: can it be used again? Can it be fixed? I'm made of reused parts myself! Come to my workshop.

          Transformation workshop

          Before recycling, you can reuse: use again, fix and transform. In Tampinha's workshop, choose a project and take the right materials from the shelf to build it. Build 3 projects to earn the star.

          1. Choose a project

          Workshop safety. Ask an adult for help with cutting and making holes. A cut bottle has an edge that can hurt: the adult covers it with tape. Wash and dry packaging before using it. Never use medicine or cleaning product packaging. Small parts, bottle caps and cords are not for children under 3 (SOCIEDADE BRASILEIRA DE PEDIATRIA, 2014).

          2. Take the materials from the shelf All clean and dry

          Made by me: 0 of 5

            What comes first?

            Brazilian law has an order of priority for waste: first, don't create it; then reduce, reuse, recycle and treat it. Only at the very end comes the final disposal of landfill waste (BRASIL, 2010).

            Theme 4

            I take care

            The best waste is the waste that never even exists! To create less, there are the 5 Rs: rethink, reduce, reuse, recycle and refuse (BRASIL, 2013).

            • RethinkDo I really need this?
            • ReduceUse only what you need.
            • ReuseUse again, fix and transform.
            • RecycleSort it so it becomes a new product.
            • RefuseSay no to what harms the environment.

            The 5 Rs

            There are 8 actions per round. Read each one and say which of the 5 Rs it puts into practice. Get 6 right to earn the star.

            The 5 Rs were adapted from the A3P program of Brazil's Ministry of the Environment (BRASIL, 2013).

            Snack time! Packaging, straws, napkins: recess can create a lot of waste. Or almost none! It depends on what goes in the lunchbox.

                      Credits

                      About the project

                      The Outreach Project Urban and Environmental Literacy (Alfabetismo e Letramento Urbano e Ambiental) is an initiative of the Graduate Program in Architecture and Urbanism at UNIVAG (PPGAU-UNIVAG), carried out in partnership with ANAP – Associação Amigos da Natureza da Alta Paulista and linked to the Research Group City, Society and Landscape (Cidade, Sociedade e Paisagem).

                      The project aims to bring the university, schools and society closer together, spreading and popularizing scientific knowledge about cities, the environment, landscape and sustainability in language that children can understand.

                      Basic urban and environmental literacy refers to a child's ability to know, recognize and understand the basic elements, concepts and processes related to the city and the environment. It is building the repertoire a child needs to be able to “read” the place where they live.

                      Urban and environmental literacy in practice is the next step: it refers to the ability to use this knowledge to interpret, connect, question and take a stand on real situations in their area, and even to propose solutions and take part in actions that bring change.

                      One of the project's products is ECO LEGAL Interactive, a digital educational publication whose issues turn knowledge and findings from undergraduate research, master's dissertations, faculty research and postdoctoral studies into interactive content for children.

                      Each issue covers a specific theme, combining scientific knowledge, educational language, visuals, games and activities to help develop urban and environmental literacy.

                      In this issue

                      This issue is about urban solid waste: what it is, where materials come from, how to sort it, how waste is transformed through recycling, composting and reuse, and how each of us can create less.

                      Issue summary

                      Theme

                      The issue is about urban solid waste, organized into four themes: “I know” (the difference between waste and landfill waste, where materials come from, and microplastics); “I sort” (recycling collection, waste that has its own drop-off point, and the work of waste pickers); “I transform” (recycling, composting and reuse); and “I take care” (the 5 Rs and everyday consumer choices). The 2030 Agenda core is SDG 12, Responsible consumption and production.

                      Objective

                      To help children understand that almost everything thrown away still has value when it is sorted and sent to the right place, and to recognize that each person's consumer choices change the amount of waste the city creates.

                      Specific objectives

                      • Tell waste apart from landfill waste and classify urban solid waste into dry recyclables, organic waste and landfill waste.
                      • Relate everyday objects to the raw material they are made from and recognize that plastic thrown away in the wrong place breaks down into microplastics.
                      • Sort waste for recycling collection and identify the items that have their own drop-off point, such as batteries, medicine, electronics, light bulbs, cooking oil and tires.
                      • Recognize the work of waste pickers and the stages that take sorted material back to industry.
                      • Understand recycling, composting and reuse as ways of transforming waste.
                      • Apply the 5 Rs, Rethink, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Refuse (BRASIL, 2013), to everyday situations.

                      Methodology

                      The issue adopts game-based learning, in three moments that repeat in each section: the mascot introduces the theme in a short speech, with the key words highlighted; the child plays, tests hypotheses and makes decisions; and each answer gets feedback that explains why, so that mistakes also teach.

                      The activities follow the progression of urban and environmental literacy: identifying the elements, understanding the relationships between them, deciding and taking part. In this issue, the path follows four verbs, get to know, sort, transform and take care: children start with the names and origins of things, move on to sorting and the work of those who recycle, follow how materials are transformed and end with their own consumer choices.

                      The language is simple, the drawings are stylized, and there are accessibility features: audio of the speech and instructions, and translation into Libras (Brazilian Sign Language) via the VLibras Suite in the Portuguese version. Progress is tracked with stars and ends with the mission of the week, to do at home, and the diploma. The issue is aligned with the BNCC skills (BRASIL, 2018) and the 2030 Agenda targets (NAÇÕES UNIDAS, 2015), listed in the panels below.

                      Rationale for the activities

                      Trash or waste? and Where does it come from?
                      They build the issue's vocabulary. In the first, children classify waste into dry recyclables, organic waste and landfill waste and see that only landfill waste can't be used anymore (BRASIL, 2010). In the second, they link each object to the place in nature its raw material comes from, which makes saving and reusing materials meaningful.
                      Microplastic detectives
                      It deals with waste that escapes collection. Children investigate seven clues in a scene and find out where microplastics come from, how they reach rivers and the sea, and where they have been found. On health effects, the activity only says that scientists are still studying the subject.
                      The colors of recycling and Proper disposal
                      They practice sorting. In the first, children take each item to the bin of the right color, following the national color code (CONSELHO NACIONAL DO MEIO AMBIENTE, 2001), and are told that the rule may change from city to city. In the second, they learn about waste that doesn't go in regular collection and where an adult should drop off each item.
                      At the cooperative
                      It puts children in the place of waste pickers, in three stages: sorting, pressing and selling. The activity presents this work as a recognized occupation and shows that the income from sales is shared among the cooperative's members.
                      From used to new and From peel to fertilizer
                      They show transformation. In the first, children choose a material (PET bottle, aluminum can, paper or glass) and put in order the six stages of the path it takes to become a new product. In the second, they look after a compost bin: they choose what goes in, balance the layers of wet waste and dry material and follow the work of earthworms, bacteria and fungi (BRASIL, 2017; ANJOS, 2015).
                      Transformation workshop
                      It reminds us that reuse comes before recycling. Children choose a project, select the right materials to build it and get safety guidance, including asking an adult for help with cutting and making holes.
                      The 5 Rs and My lunchbox
                      They move from disposal to prevention. In the first, children match actions to each of the 5 Rs: Rethink, Reduce, Reuse, Recycle and Refuse (BRASIL, 2013). In the second, they apply the idea to a decision from their own daily life: they pack the school snack and see what's left after recess.
                      Challenge: a day with less waste
                      This is the summary activity. At eight stops, from morning to night, children choose between three actions and see the result of each choice in the day's bag. When a choice creates waste, the feedback shows another path and the matching R.
                      Quiz, Word search and Memory game
                      They review and reinforce the issue's vocabulary and concepts.
                      SDGs and the 2030 Agenda

                      The 2030 Agenda brings together 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and 169 targets, adopted by the 193 Member States of the United Nations in 2015 (NAÇÕES UNIDAS, 2015). SDG 12 is the core of this issue, through the target of reducing waste generation through prevention, reduction, recycling and reuse, and five other goals connect with it.

                      • 12Responsible consumption and production

                        SDG 12Responsible consumption and production

                        • Target 12.5By 2030, substantially reduce waste generation through prevention, reduction, recycling and reuse.
                        • Target 12.3By 2030, halve per capita global food waste at the retail and consumer levels and reduce food losses along production and supply chains, including post-harvest losses.
                        • Target 12.8By 2030, ensure that people everywhere have the relevant information and awareness for sustainable development and lifestyles in harmony with nature.
                        • Target 12.2By 2030, achieve the sustainable management and efficient use of natural resources.
                        • Target 12.4By 2020, achieve the environmentally sound management of chemicals and all wastes throughout their life cycle, in accordance with agreed international frameworks, and significantly reduce their release to air, water and soil in order to minimize their adverse impacts on human health and the environment.

                      BNCC

                      Skills from Brazil's National Common Core Curriculum (Base Nacional Comum Curricular, BNCC) (BRASIL, 2018) that this issue's activities help develop, from 1st to 5th grade, with one 9th-grade skill for older classes. Each skill comes with the official text and the activities where it is practiced. Tap a code to see the skill highlighted.
